title: eofs: A Library for EOF Analysis of Meteorological, Oceanographic, and Climate Data
abstract: The eofs library provides a high-level Python interface for computing empirical orthogonal functions (EOFs) and related quantities, with a focus on correctness and ease of use. The library is implemented in a modular hierarchical fashion, allowing computations using plain arrays, or the inclusion of metadata. The software provides a convenient package for users wanting to perform EOF analysis in Python, and integrates with popular libraries from atmospheric and climate science. The software is available on Github.

narrative:
Short impact summary

eofs has achieved clear scholarly uptake as a practical Python tool for empirical orthogonal function analysis in meteorology, oceanography, and climate science. It has been cited 185 times, placing it in the top 10% of works for its field and year, and it also shows substantial downstream reuse across articles, preprints, reviews, conference papers, and dissertations.

Full narrative

Published in the Journal of Open Research Software in 2016, eofs addresses a specific methodological need: a high-level, user-friendly Python interface for EOF analysis that emphasizes correctness, modular design, and support for metadata-aware workflows. The article’s impact record shows that this software-oriented contribution has been taken up well beyond its original venue, with citations accumulating steadily over time and reaching a broad climate-science audience.

The citation landscape is especially strong in core atmospheric, oceanographic, and climate journals. Recent and repeated citing venues include Geophysical Research Letters, Journal of Climate, Quarterly Journal of the Royal Meteorological Society, Climate Dynamics, International Journal of Climatology, and Geoscientific Model Development. That pattern suggests the library is being used not just as a general programming resource, but as infrastructure within active research workflows for climate variability, meteorological simulation, and oceanographic analysis.

Downstream reuse reinforces that picture. The record shows 187 documented reuse instances, dominated by journal articles but also including peer review reports, preprints, conference papers, and dissertations. The reuse profile is geographically and institutionally broad, with contributions from the United States, the United Kingdom, China, Germany, and other countries, and with especially visible uptake in education and government-linked settings. Taken together, these signals indicate that eofs has become a routine analytical component in the research ecosystem rather than a one-off reference.

The wider attention record is more modest than the citation record: there are no captured event-data mentions or scite citation classifications in the available sources. Even so, the combination of sustained citations, field-leading venue placement, and repeated reuse suggests durable scholarly value. In practical terms, eofs appears to have helped standardize and simplify a widely used climate-analysis technique for Python-based research communities.
